title: Files: formats, failures, and explicit saving
lead: Validate an import, create a report, and separately confirm transfer of runtime output into the project.
why: A written message does not establish persistence. You need stream checks, an explicit format, the resulting artifact, and a clear boundary between the sandbox and a personal project.
objectives: Explain: A file as a resource
Trace: The format is an interface
Implement and verify the lab against its exact contract.
Identify a common defect: Do not open the input with ofstream before validation. Do not assume ambient runtime persistence between runs.
prerequisites: Modules 1–2: expressions, comparisons, types, references, and checked cin.
Follow the prerequisite links: cpp.multifile-build, cpp.streams-state. New constructs are introduced before the assignment.

sections.title: A file as a resource
paragraphs: ifstream from <fstream> reads a file; ofstream writes one. Construction associates the stream with a path, and destruction closes the resource. Check opening through bool(stream). RAII cleanup is useful, but successful opening does not guarantee every later operation succeeds.
A regular ofstream may truncate an existing file. Do not open an input file for writing before validating its data. The lab writes a separate report.txt and preserves records.txt.

sections.title: The format is an interface
paragraphs: A text format defines encoding, delimiters, field counts, and bounds. The lab records.txt contains one integer in -1000…1000 per line, at most 100 lines of 200 bytes. An empty file is valid; a blank line is malformed.

Parse each line using a local istringstream and reject trailing data. Do not save a struct by dumping its memory: padding, type sizes, and byte order may differ. A textual contract is easier to verify manually and with two compilers.

sections.title: Read and write failures
paragraphs: A missing file produces missing; a malformed record produces invalid. Do not treat every stopped getline as normal completion: check bad and unexpected failure without eof. A partial import must not generate a successful final report.

After writing, call close and check the stream: flushing can fail late. The lab distinguishes write-error from invalid. This does not promise atomic replacement after a crash; that needs a separate storage strategy.

sections.title: The Nexus virtual filesystem
paragraphs: A program sees relative files supplied with its request. Absolute paths, .., and system directories are unavailable. Every run receives a fresh runtime filesystem; a previous run’s file does not appear automatically in the next. stdin is not a substitute for testing file input.

Limits are 128 files, 512 KiB per file, 2 MiB for input and runtime files, and 2 MiB of writes per run. Exceeding them is a provider limitation distinct from an algorithm defect. Do not raise quotas to bypass an exercise.

sections.title: An artifact and a personal project
paragraphs: The result panel lists new or changed runtime files. Downloading saves a separate copy. Saving text results transfers them into the VFS only through an explicit action and when no conflicting edits exist. A program cannot silently replace source code.

A binary result downloads as bytes rather than becoming an editor text file. A conflict preserves the project source. For another run, explicitly save a permitted text file, then rerun the reader and compare contents.

sections.title: Roundtrip evidence
paragraphs: Separately test a missing file, a valid import, malformed data, export, and report.txt contents. Then confirm saving into the project and a fresh run. Reading within the same run does not establish that final step.

Use synthetic data only; do not put keys or personal work into evidence. Next, a linked list demonstrates node-resource management, while the final project combines records, commands, tests, and file formats.
